title: Asha and the Breathing Weather Tower
markdown:
Sunlight burst through Asha's window, bright and bold. Something still felt off. No wind whispered. The dune was too quiet.

"Odd," Asha mumbled, brain already buzzing. Today was the day. Her Weather Tower, perched high on the sand, was ready — except its spinner sat stuck, and its vane hung limp.

A happy bark. Drift, the plumpest seal, waddled up, Gran Mae behind him.

"Morning, Asha." Gran Mae's voice was warm. "What a still morning. I hoped for a good bluster for these biscuits."

Drift gave a hopeful woof at the word biscuits.

Asha dashed out. "The tower isn't working. The spinner won't spin."

"Perhaps it's waiting for something," Gran Mae suggested, kindly enough that it did not feel like a riddle.

Asha sprinted. Drift bounded close. She touched a gauge. "It's cold. And look — water dots, stuck. Not dripping."

The metal had the chill of a thing that had sat sealed. Drift nudged a loose panel. Whoosh — a puff of air escaped. The water dots jiggled.

"You saw that?" Asha's voice shot up. "Air was trapped in there. When you nudged it, it got a way out."

She traced the tower with both hands. "This part has holes. This part is solid. The spinner and the vane need the outside air to reach them. If the air is locked in, damp and still, they can't tell us anything — even if a breeze is trying."

Drift nosed other panels. Whoosh. Puff. Asha's gaze landed on a vent, half-twisted shut. "This. If I open it just so…"

She turned the dial. Trapped dampness sighed out. The stuck droplets began to run. The spinner, which had been glued by cold wet, gave a tiny tick.

Then a real gust came off the sea, the kind that had been waiting just beyond the dune. With a speedy whir the spinner spun, faster, faster. The vane swung firmly into the salt. A cheerful ding-ding-ding chimed. Wind whipped Asha's hair and brought the ocean with it.

The instruments had not made the wind. They had been allowed to feel it.

Gran Mae beamed. "You did it."

"It's air pressure, isn't it?" Asha grinned, still tasting salt. "Still air sits heavy. When the pressure is different from one place to another, air moves — that's wind. The tower has to breathe so that moving air can push the spinner and turn the vane. Sealed, it only knew its own trapped puff. Open, it can report the weather."

Drift barked and chased the playful breeze, as if he had invented it.

"Exactly." Gran Mae broke a biscuit. "The world's full of puzzles that look broken until they can inhale."

Asha stood tall in the wind. She did not wonder what other secrets hid in the gust. She watched the vane hold its line, then glance, then hold again.

"I wonder," she said, "whether tomorrow's biscuits will want a north wind or a south — and whether the gauge will tell us before we feel it on our faces."

Gran Mae's eyes crinkled. Drift voted, with his whole body, for whichever wind came with crumbs.
